list_servers.title: List logical SQL servers in the subscription
list_servers.description: Every Azure SQL logical server in the subscription, with its `fullyQualifiedDomainName` (the host in a connection string), its administrator login, version and public network access setting. Databases hang off servers, so this is the first call in almost every workflow here.

expand.description: Child resources to include, e.g. databases or elasticPools.

output.description: Every logical SQL server in the subscription.

items.description: id, name, location and properties (fullyQualifiedDomainName, administratorLogin, version, state, publicNetworkAccess, minimalTlsVersion).

list_servers_in_group.title: List SQL servers in a resource group
list_servers_in_group.description: The logical SQL servers in one resource group. Cheaper than scanning the subscription when the group is known.

resource_group.description: The resource group to look in.

get_server.title: Get a logical SQL server
get_server.description: One server in full: its fully qualified domain name, admin login, minimum TLS version, whether public network access is enabled, and its Entra ID administrator. `publicNetworkAccess` set to Disabled means only private endpoints can reach it, no matter what the firewall rules say.

server_name.description: The logical server name, without the .database.windows.net suffix.

properties.description: fullyQualifiedDomainName, administratorLogin, version, state, publicNetworkAccess, minimalTlsVersion and administrators.

update_server.title: Patch a SQL server's settings
update_server.description:
Merge a change into a server -- rotate the administrator password, change the minimum TLS version, turn public network access on or off, set tags. Everything not mentioned is left alone.
Disabling public network access cuts off every client not coming through a private endpoint, immediately. Changing the admin password breaks anything still using the old one.
update_server.notes: Disabling publicNetworkAccess or rotating the admin password takes effect immediately.

administrator_login_password.description: A new password for the SQL administrator login. Breaks existing connection strings.

minimal_tls_version.description: Lowest TLS version the server accepts.

public_network_access.description: Disabled restricts the server to private endpoints only.

list_databases.title: List the databases on a server
list_databases.description:
Every database on one logical server, with its SKU, size limits, status, collation and creation date. The `master` database appears in the list and is not a user database -- ignore it.
`status` of `Paused` means a serverless database has auto-paused; the next connection resumes it, with a cold-start delay of a few seconds.

items.description: id, name, location, sku and properties (status, collation, maxSizeBytes, currentServiceObjectiveName, creationDate, earliestRestoreDate).

get_database.title: Get a database
get_database.description: One database's tier and size, its status, its collation, its zone redundancy and -- the field that matters for recovery -- `earliestRestoreDate`, which is the oldest point restore_database can take you back to. Anything before it is gone.

sku.description: name, tier, family and capacity -- the service objective.

properties.description: status, collation, maxSizeBytes, currentServiceObjectiveName, earliestRestoreDate, zoneRedundant and licenseType.

create_or_update_database.title: Create a database
create_or_update_database.description:
Create a database on a logical server, or replace an existing one's configuration. The SKU decides both the cost and the capabilities: `GP_S_Gen5_2` is a serverless General Purpose database that auto-pauses, `GP_Gen5_2` a provisioned one, `HS_Gen5_2` Hyperscale, `Basic` and `S0`/`P1` the older DTU tiers.
Creation is asynchronous -- poll get_database until `status` is `Online`. To copy an existing database instead of creating an empty one, set create_mode to Copy and point source_database_id at it.
create_or_update_database.notes: The SKU determines the bill. Serverless (GP_S_*) tiers auto-pause; provisioned ones bill continuously.

server_name.description: The logical server to create the database on.

location.description: The region -- must match the server's.

sku_name.description: Service objective, e.g. GP_S_Gen5_2 (serverless), GP_Gen5_2, HS_Gen5_2, S0 or Basic.

sku_tier.description: Service tier, e.g. GeneralPurpose, BusinessCritical, Hyperscale, Standard or Basic.

sku_capacity.description: vCores or DTUs, matching the SKU family.

max_size_bytes.description: Maximum database size in bytes, e.g. 34359738368 for 32 GB.

zone_redundant.description: Spread replicas across availability zones. Not available on every tier.

create_mode.description: Default creates an empty database. Copy duplicates source_database_id. Secondary creates a geo-replica of it.

source_database_id.description: ARM id of the database to copy or replicate, when create_mode needs one.

elastic_pool_id.description: ARM id of an elastic pool to place the database in instead of giving it its own SKU.

output.description: The database as created; creation continues asynchronously.

sku.description: The service objective it was created at.

properties.description: status -- Creating at this point -- and the resolved settings.

update_database.title: Scale or reconfigure a database
update_database.description:
Change a database's service objective, maximum size, elastic pool membership or tags, leaving everything else alone. This is how you scale Azure SQL up and down.
A tier change is online but not instant -- the database stays available while Azure moves it, and `status` reports `Scaling` meanwhile. Scaling down below the data already stored fails, and moving between tier families (DTU to vCore, or into Hyperscale) is one-way for Hyperscale.
update_database.notes: Billing changes as soon as the new tier is applied. Moving into Hyperscale cannot be undone.

sku_name.description: The new service objective, e.g. GP_Gen5_4.

sku_capacity.description: The new vCore or DTU count.

max_size_bytes.description: New maximum size in bytes. Cannot go below the data already stored.

elastic_pool_id.description: ARM id of an elastic pool to move the database into.

auto_pause_delay.description: Minutes of inactivity before a serverless database auto-pauses. -1 disables auto-pause.

min_capacity.description: Minimum vCores a serverless database scales down to, e.g. 0.5.

properties.description: status -- Scaling while the change lands.

delete_database.title: Delete a database
delete_database.description:
Drop a database. Not immediately final: Azure keeps a restorable copy for the backup retention period, and list_restorable_dropped_databases shows it, so restore_deleted_database can bring it back under a new name.
That safety net disappears if the SERVER is deleted, and it does not exist at all for a database that never had backups configured.
delete_database.notes: Recoverable with restore_deleted_database for the retention period, unless the server is also deleted.

pause_database.title: Pause a Data Warehouse database
pause_database.description:
Pause a dedicated SQL pool (Data Warehouse) so it stops billing for compute; storage keeps billing. Only applies to DataWarehouse-tier databases -- a normal Azure SQL database has no pause, and a serverless one pauses itself after its auto_pause_delay.
Resume with resume_database before connecting again.

database_name.description: The Data Warehouse database to pause.

resume_database.title: Resume a paused Data Warehouse database
resume_database.description: Bring a paused dedicated SQL pool back online. Asynchronous and not instant -- poll get_database until `status` is `Online` before pointing anything at it.

restore_database.title: Restore a database to a point in time
restore_database.description:
Create a NEW database from an existing one's continuous backups, as it stood at a given instant. Nothing is overwritten: the source database keeps running and the restore lands under the name you give, which is what makes this safe to reach for during an incident.
`restore_point_in_time` must be at or after the source's `earliestRestoreDate` (from get_database) and no later than now. Restores take minutes to hours depending on size -- poll get_database on the new name until `status` is `Online`.
restore_database.notes: Creates a new database rather than overwriting the source. Bills as a second database.

target_database_name.description: The name for the restored copy. Must not already exist.

source_database_id.description: ARM id of the database to restore from, from get_database.

restore_point_in_time.description: The instant to restore to, ISO 8601 UTC. Must be at or after the source's earliestRestoreDate.

output.description: The restored database, still being created.

properties.description: status -- Creating while the restore runs.

list_restorable_dropped_databases.title: List databases that were deleted but can still be restored
list_restorable_dropped_databases.description: Databases dropped from a server that are still inside their backup retention window, each with its deletion date and its `earliestRestoreDate`. The first call after "someone deleted the database" -- the entries here are exactly what restore_deleted_database can bring back, and an empty list means the window has closed.

server_name.description: The logical server the database was on.

output.description: Deleted databases still inside their retention window.

items.description: id, name, sku and properties (databaseName, deletionDate, creationDate, earliestRestoreDate, maxSizeBytes).

restore_deleted_database.title: Restore a deleted database
restore_deleted_database.description:
Bring back a dropped database from its backups, as a new database on the same server. `source_database_id` is the `id` from list_restorable_dropped_databases, which includes the deletion timestamp and is not the same as the original database's id.
Restores to the name you give -- reusing the original name only works if nothing has since taken it.

server_name.description: The logical server to restore onto.

target_database_name.description: The name to restore the database under.

source_database_id.description: The restorable dropped database's id, exactly as list_restorable_dropped_databases returns it.

restore_point_in_time.description: An instant before the deletion to restore to, ISO 8601 UTC. Omit for the state at the moment of deletion.

output.description: The restored database, still being created.

properties.description: status -- Creating while the restore runs.

get_backup_retention_policy.title: Get a database's backup retention
get_backup_retention_policy.description: How many days of continuous (point-in-time) backup a database keeps, and whether the differential backups run every 12 or 24 hours. This number is the width of the restore_database window -- 7 days by default, up to 35. Anything older needs a long-term retention policy, which is separate.

set_backup_retention_policy.title: Set a database's backup retention
set_backup_retention_policy.description: Change how many days of point-in-time restore a database keeps, from 1 to 35. Widening the window costs more storage; narrowing it DISCARDS backups beyond the new limit, which shortens how far restore_database can reach -- that part is not reversible.
set_backup_retention_policy.notes: Reducing retention permanently discards backups older than the new window.

retention_days.description: Days of point-in-time restore to keep, 1 to 35.

diff_backup_interval_hours.description: How often differential backups run. 12 gives a finer restore granularity than 24.

list_firewall_rules.title: List a server's firewall rules
list_firewall_rules.description:
The IP ranges allowed to reach a logical server. This is the first thing to check when a connection fails with something that looks like a timeout or an "is not allowed to access the server" error rather than a bad password.
A rule with start and end both `0.0.0.0` is the special "AllowAllWindowsAzureIps" rule: it permits other Azure services, not the whole internet. A rule of `0.0.0.0` to `255.255.255.255` does permit the whole internet, and is almost always a mistake.

create_firewall_rule.title: Allow an IP range through a server's firewall
create_firewall_rule.description:
Open a server to a range of client IPs. Keep the range as narrow as the client actually needs -- a rule of 0.0.0.0 to 255.255.255.255 exposes the server to every address on the internet, leaving only the password between an attacker and the data.
Passing 0.0.0.0 for both addresses is the special case that allows other Azure services rather than an actual address. Reusing an existing rule name replaces that rule.
create_firewall_rule.notes: Widening the range widens the attack surface. This grants network reach, not database permissions.

rule_name.description: A name for the rule. Reusing a name replaces that rule.

start_ip_address.description: First address in the allowed range.

end_ip_address.description: Last address in the allowed range. Same as the start for a single address.

delete_firewall_rule.title: Remove a firewall rule
delete_firewall_rule.description: Close a previously allowed IP range. Anything connecting from that range loses access on its next connection attempt -- existing connections are not cut, which can make the effect look delayed. Check list_firewall_rules first to be sure which clients the rule was carrying.

list_elastic_pools.title: List elastic pools on a server
list_elastic_pools.description: The elastic pools on a logical server, with each pool's SKU, per-database minimum and maximum capacity, and storage limit. A pool shares one budget of compute across many databases, which is cheaper than provisioning each one when their peaks do not coincide.

items.description: id, name, sku and properties (state, maxSizeBytes, perDatabaseSettings, zoneRedundant).

list_database_usages.title: Get a database's resource usage
list_database_usages.description: Current usage against a database's limits -- storage used against its maximum, and the metrics whose exhaustion causes throttling. A database that has hit its size limit refuses INSERTs with an error that does not obviously say so; this is where that shows up.

items.description: name, displayName, currentValue, limit and unit.

list_server_usages.title: Get a server's resource usage
list_server_usages.description: Server-level usage against quota -- notably the DTU or vCore budget shared across its databases. Worth reading before adding another database to a busy server.

output.description: Server usage metrics against their limits.

items.description: name, resourceName, displayName, currentValue, limit and unit.

list_database_advisors.title: Get Azure's tuning advice for a database
list_database_advisors.description:
Azure SQL's own automatic tuning advisors -- create index, drop index, fix schema issues, force last good plan -- each with its status and whether it is set to apply automatically or wait for approval.
This is the closest thing here to "why is my database slow", and it is based on the workload Azure has actually observed rather than on guesswork. Expand recommendedActions to see the individual suggestions.

expand.description: Set to recommendedActions to include the individual suggestions.

output.description: The database's tuning advisors and their advice.

items.description: name and properties (advisorStatus, autoExecuteStatus, lastChecked, recommendedActions when expanded).
